overview: Castlerock's beach runs for about a kilometre between the sea cliffs of Downhill to the west and the Barmouth, where the River Bann meets the sea, to the east. The village sits right behind it, and Castlerock Golf Club fills the dunes east of the entrance. The beach regularly holds a Blue Flag. On clear days you can look west to the Inishowen peninsula in Donegal.

Four boardwalks lead from the free promenade parking through the dunes, which are protected as a Special Area of Conservation. These dunes run upstream along the estuary to Grangemore, where the National Trust has a bird sanctuary, and include some of the oldest dated dunes in Ireland. Harbour porpoises and seals are often seen feeding in the estuary at the Barmouth, and there is on-site information about the dunes.

It is a quieter base than Portrush, with its own railway station on the Coleraine–Derry~Londonderry line and a regular Blue Flag. Cars can drive onto the eastern part of the beach all year, but wind-blown sand can make it hard going. The concrete pier at the Barmouth is open to walkers and anglers, but the council advises extreme care and says to avoid it in high winds or breaking swell.
suits: Surfers who bring their own kit
notFor: Anyone tempted to surf near the Barmouth

text: Castlerock is an exposed beach and jetty break with lefts and rights. Forecast sites rate it best on a north-westerly groundswell with offshore winds from the south, and best around mid tide. It is fairly consistent outside summer and is rarely crowded even when it's working.
The Bann estuary is the big thing to understand: keep well away from the river mouth and the pier. Use the flagged zones when lifeguards are on duty in July and August.

The break sits by the Barmouth jetties at the mouth of the River Bann, with a long right on the Castlerock side and a left towards Portstewart. It wants a north-westerly to northerly swell from about 2ft up to 8ft, with a southerly wind offshore, and it works at all stages of the tide: mid-tide is the pick on medium swells, when the Barmouth banks light up.

Past about 8ft it turns rippy and starts to close out, and the water quality near the river mouth can be questionable. Winter is the best season, with February the cleanest month in forecast data, and it's rarely crowded. On small days the waves can be gentle and long, which suits longboards, but keep well clear of the jetties and the river mouth.

cards.title: Improvers and up
cards.text: No school on site; learners should book elsewhere.

cards.label: Conditions
cards.title: NW swell, south wind, mid tide
cards.text: 2 to 8ft; the Barmouth banks work best on medium swells.

cards.label: Season
cards.title: Winter
cards.text: February is cleanest in forecast data; summer is often flat.

cards.label: Hazards
cards.title: Bann estuary
cards.text: River and tidal currents near the Barmouth jetties; it closes out and gets rippy past 8ft.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Free promenade
practical.text: Free parking on the promenade; cars may also drive onto the eastern beach year-round.

practical.label: Facilities
practical.title: Promenade
practical.text: Accessible toilets and accessible parking on the promenade.

practical.label: Lifeguards
practical.title: Seasonal RNLI patrol
practical.text: The council lists a seasonal RNLI patrol, 10am–6pm daily in July and August. Check the RNLI site for this year's dates.

practical.label: Dogs & horses
practical.title: Summer restrictions
practical.text: The council allows dogs but applies restrictions from 1 June to 15 September — check the signs at the entrance for where they apply. From 1 May to 30 September horse riding is only allowed before 11am and after 7pm.

practical.label: Rail
practical.title: Castlerock station
practical.text: On the line between Coleraine and Derry~Londonderry.

faqs.q: Is it safe near the river mouth?
faqs.a: No — keep well clear. The council advises extreme care on the Barmouth pier and not to walk it in high winds or breaking swell.
Forecast sites rate a north-westerly swell, southerly wind and mid tide.
Harbour porpoises and seals feed in the estuary at the Barmouth.
